one_liner: Python tool that turns a trained Keras MLP/CNN into one dependency-free C++ header; snippet-reported 2-25x over Keras eager on one core.
what_it_does: CodeJeNN reads Keras models saved as .h5 or .keras (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX backend) and writes a C++ header per model with all weights inlined, so a solver (CFD, constitutive laws, reduced-order models) can call the network without linking an ML runtime. The API is a single function template named after the model file, e.g. model<double>(const std::array<double, N>&), returning a std::array; inputs and outputs can be min-max or mean-std normalized from .npy files. It is not a drop-in for Keras: you change the call site, regenerate the header whenever the model changes, and supply C++ code yourself for custom activations.
how_it_is_fast: It removes the framework entirely: no Python dispatch, no tensor allocation and no graph runtime per call, which is what dominates single-sample inference of small models in Keras eager mode. Weights are emitted as constexpr std::array literals, layers are small inline function templates (a plain scalar dot-product loop for Dense) with activations passed as lambdas so the compiler can inline everything, and intermediate buffers are preallocated function-local statics. The README says vectorization and threading are deliberately left out, on the assumption that the host solver is already parallel.
when_to_use: Calling a small Keras-trained MLP or CNN once per cell or per sample inside a C++ physics or CFD code, where linking TensorFlow, libtorch or ONNX Runtime is unwanted
Single-sample, single-thread latency on CPU with models small enough that the weight arrays stay in cache (the speed test uses a 1000-64-32-100 MLP and a 10x100 input CNN)
Supported layer sets only: Dense, Conv1D/2D/3D and their transposes, separable and depthwise conv, pooling, Batch/Layer/Unit/Group normalization, Reshape/Flatten/Rescaling, common activations
Research or government projects that can accept the NRL Open License Agreement
when_not_to_use: Calling the generated function more than once with a 1-D output and no output normalization file: the generator emits `static std::array<Scalar, N> model_output = layer_K_output;`, a static local initialized only on the first call, so every later call returns the first result (this is the configuration of both speed-test models)
Multithreaded callers: every layer buffer and the output are function-local statics, so concurrent calls from OpenMP or MPI+threads code race

Large models or batched throughput: Dense is an unvectorized scalar loop with strided weight access, the README warns large static arrays make it memory-bandwidth bound, and against Keras JIT the snippet-reported gain is only about 2-2.5x
Recurrent, attention or multi-input/multi-output models: only single-input, single-output sequential or functional MLP/CNN graphs are supported (ConvLSTM2D is commented out)

Projects needing an OSI license: the NRL agreement restricts redistribution to its own terms, takes an irrevocable grant-back of modifications to the US Government, and can be terminated by the Government

integration.form: source-drop (generated single header per model; the generator is a Python script, src/api-core/main.py)
integration.dependencies: none for the generated header beyond the C++ standard library; the generator needs Keras plus a backend (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX), matplotlib, pandas, scikit-learn, sympy, spektral, pydot
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; the generated code uses constexpr std::array and generic lambdas (C++17 is a safe assumption, not stated). The speed test used Homebrew g++-15 with -O3 -march=native -ffast-math
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++ compiler (portable scalar code, no intrinsics); tested by the author on an Apple M1 Pro
integration.thread_safety: not thread-safe: generated functions keep layer outputs and the returned array in function-local static buffers

gotchas: Stale-output bug: with a 1-D output and no output_*.npy normalization files, the returned array is a static initialized once, so results after the first call are wrong; the --debug comparison calls the model once and does not catch it, and the speed test discards results
Weights are non-static constexpr locals inside the inline function; for large models check stack use and code size, since the compiler may materialize them per call
Custom activations need a hand-written C++ version pasted into the header; until then the header prints 'WARNING: CUSTOM ACTIVATION HAS NOT BEEN IMPLEMENTED' on every call

Docs disagree with the scripts: the speed-test readme says the CNN used PyTorch and the MLP TensorFlow, but the checked-in test.py files set the opposite; src/generate.sh passes --double, which main.py's argparse does not define (it takes --bit=32|64), so the shipped default script should exit with an unrecognized-argument error
pick_this_over_siblings_when: RTNeural is the catalogued alternative for small-model C++ inference, with measured comparisons against libtorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite; pick CodeJeNN only when you want a single dependency-free header generated straight from a Keras .h5/.keras file, including 3D and transposed convolutions, and can accept the NRL license and fix the static-buffer issues. Kaoken and tiny-ml-runtime take the same baked-weights approach for other model types.
verified_claims_summary: The repo's speed test (tutorials/06_speed_test) times 10,000 single-sample calls of a small MLP and CNN in Keras eager or JIT mode against the generated C++ (g++-15 -O3 -march=native -ffast-math, one thread, MacBook M1 Pro) but publishes no numbers. The figures come only from search snippets of arXiv 2607.02746: MLP 0.48 s vs 12.01 s Keras/TensorFlow eager (about 25x) and 1.21 s with JIT (about 2.5x), CNN 1.05 s vs 19.14 s eager (about 18x) and 2.17 s JIT (about 2.1x). The C++ timing loop discards outputs, and the measured models hit the stale-output code path described above.
status_note: A single-commit code drop (2026-06-22, 'final draft for paper') from a US Naval Research Laboratory project with 1 star; the NRL Open License makes it reference-only for this catalog, and the generated header may count as a derivative work under that agreement.
